extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of literature, poetry, painting, architecture, and aesthetics; creative writers and artists seeking principles for producing the sublime
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and sources that produce the feeling of the sublime in art, literature, architecture, and sensory experience—what qualities (power, vastness, darkness, sound, etc.) affect the imagination to create awe or terror. Useful for writers, poets, painters, and architects aiming to craft grand or sublime effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of vast power is a prime source of the sublime because power is typically associated with the ability to inflict pain and death; strength united with the possibility of harm produces terror and hence sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize danger, uncontrollability, or superior force (e.g., lions, tigers, leviathan, or sovereigns called 'dread majesty'). Power that is harmless or subservient (an ox used for ploughing, a tame horse) loses sublimity and becomes contemptible. Use circumstances that highlight capacity for destruction or freedom from human control. Example anti-pattern: portraying strength as useful/subject-to-uselessness removes grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privation
rubrics_metrics.description: General privations—vacuum, darkness, solitude, silence—are great because they are terrible and fill the imagination with dread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imagery of emptiness (vacant houses, night, silent shades) to heighten awe. Classical examples: Virgil's opening of the Underworld, use of darkness and solitude to magnify terror. Avoid cheerfulness or bright, detailed description where the aim is solemn sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vastness (Greatness of Dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness of dimension—length, height, depth—produces the sublime; different modes of extension have different force (height and depth often stronger than length).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer vertical or deep perspectives (precipices, towers, mountains) over mere horizontal extension. Rugged, broken surfaces have stronger sublime effects than smooth ones. Consider both extremes: extreme littleness (the infinitely small) can produce a similar effect by overwhelming the imagination with divisibility. Avoid mere gigantism without qualitative features; the way magnitude is presented matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinity fills the mind with 'delightful horror' and is a key source of the sublime—objects that seem without bounds (because the senses cannot perceive their limits) produce this effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evoking endless continuation or immeasurable scale (real or illusionary) will provoke the sublime. Use devices that remove perceptible boundaries so the imagination can extend indefinitely. Repetition and sustained sensory input can create an effect of prolongation that mimics infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession and Uniformity (artificial infinity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial infinity arises from a long succession of uniform parts such that the imagination receives uninterrupted progression and cannot find a boundary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sequences with repetition and uniformity (e.g., rotundas, long colonnades, aisles) to suggest endless extension. Avoid changes in figure, disposition, or color that interrupt progression, because each change checks the imagination. Anti-pattern: over-variety and excessive angles (cross-shaped plans) that break the illusion of continuance and diminish grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude in Building
rubrics_metrics.description: For architectural sublimity, greatness of dimension is necessary—small, few parts cannot evoke infinity; true grandeur often depends on convincing (deceptive) effects rather than mere size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for medium-long colonnades/avenues and proportion that deceives the eye into grandeur; avoid excessive length that ruins perspective and reduces perceived height. Use measured design to place the viewer in the best vantage for the sublime. Anti-pattern: buildings vast only in absolute dimensions without artistic means to sustain the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity in Pleasing Objects
rubrics_metrics.description: A related pleasure arises from perceived infinity or the promise of more (unfinished work, early spring, sketches), where the imagination is engaged by potential rather than completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pleasing or beautiful objects, leave room for imagination—suggestion, incompleteness, or promise can give pleasurable expectation. Use sketches, hints of future growth, or unfinished elements to engage the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that a work required immense labor or force confers grandeur; difficulty and the perception of huge effort increase the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the effort, force, or toil behind a work (e.g., Stonehenge's huge stones) to increase sublimity. Rudeness or lack of artifice can enhance this effect by indicating brute force rather than clever dexterity. Anti-pattern: presenting a work as trivially easy or cleverly artful reduces this source of grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence (Profusion/Multitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: A profusion of splendid, valuable, or numerous things (stars, armies, rich images) can create grandeur; apparent disorder and multitude can suggest a kind of infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mass, multiplicity, and controlled disorder to dazzle the imagination (e.g., starry heavens, thronging armies, rich poetic catalogues). In art, admit such profusion cautiously—too much splendour can impair usefulness or coherence unless it successfully presents an appearance of infinity. Examples: fireworks, certain poetic oratorical descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light (as source of the sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Light affects the sublime only when it strongly overpowers the senses (e.g., the sun) or changes rapidly; extreme light can be converted into a kind of darkness by overwhelming the eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intense light or extreme transitions between light and darkness to produce striking effects (light that overpowers, lightning's velocity). Consider contrasts—abrupt changes are more powerful than gradual ones. Avoid bland, ordinary lighting when aiming for sublime impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light in Building (architectural illumination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings intended to be sublime should generally be dark and gloomy indoors, as darkness produces stronger emotional effect than ordinary light; transitions from bright exterior to gloomy interior are effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage interior illumination to create striking transitions (from bright outdoors to dim interior) and use darkness to heighten solemnity. At night, the inverse applies: strong illumination then produces grandeur. Anti-pattern: interiors too bright in daytime when sublime darkness is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color Considered as Productive of the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Colors that are soft or cheerful are generally unfit for the sublime; sombre, fuscous colors (black, brown, deep purple) better support sublime effects. Excessive gilding, mosaics, or gay drapery tend to detract from the highest sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor dark, melancholy palettes for highest solemnity; avoid white, green, yellow, blue, pale red, or spotted hues when the aim is sustained sublimity. In many edifices where grandeur is needed but not the melancholic sublime, draw sublimity from other sources and avoid anything light and gay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and Loudness
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive loudness (cataracts, storms, thunder, artillery, shouting crowds) can overpower the soul and produce awe and terror; sounds alone (not words) can create sublime passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ overwhelming natural or mechanical sounds, collective shouting, or massive noises to astonish and confound the imagination. Use scale and intensity rather than musical nicety when the aim is terror/awe. Anti-pattern: delicate or intricate music is less effective for the sublime than sheer loudness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden beginning or cessation of a strong sound or sight rouses attention and causes a startle—this perception of danger produces terror and thus sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abrupt onsets or stops (single loud clock stroke in the night, drum beat with pauses, distant cannon) to create grand effects. Avoid smooth transitions that neutralize the faculty for sudden alarm; repetition of a strong short sound with pauses has powerful sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermitting (uncertain, tremulous sounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Low, tremulous, intermittent, or otherwise uncertain sounds can be more terrifying than total silence because they leave us anxious about their cause; uncertainty heightens fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ faint, fluctuating lights or off-and-on sounds (flickering lamp, uncertain moonlight, tremulous noises) to produce unease and imagination-driven terror. Use intermittence to maintain suspense; total predictability or full knowledge destroys the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Cries of Animals (natural inarticulate voices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sounds imitating natural cries of animals or humans in pain/danger convey strong ideas; wild animal tones (angry beasts) evoke awe and terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use animal cries and natural vocalizations to tap innate understanding of distress or threat—these modulations often communicate universally even without learned language. Avoid using the voice of creatures associated with contempt (over-familiar domestic noises) if aiming for sublimity.
